sentence: Codeine is an opioid painkiller used for pain such as pain after an operation or injury, and co-codamol is codeine combined with paracetamol for aches and pains.
note: NHS codeine: treat pain, e.g. after operation or injury; co-codamol: combines paracetamol and codeine for aches and pains.

sentence: The NHS lists constipation, drowsiness and sickness as common effects, and says it is possible to become addicted to codeine.
note: NHS side effects pages: constipation, sleepy, sick; codeine addiction possible.

sentence: Co-codamol contains paracetamol, so taking other paracetamol-containing medicines as well can lead to too much paracetamol, which can harm the liver.
note: NHS how-to page and emc leaflet: contains paracetamol, check other products; too much can cause liver damage.

sentence: Codeine is used to treat pain, for example after an operation or injury.
note: NHS codeine page summary.

sentence: Co-codamol is used for aches and pains such as period pain, muscle pain and toothache.
note: NHS About co-codamol.

sentence: Co-codamol is often used when other painkillers, such as paracetamol on its own, have not worked.
note: NHS About co-codamol.

sentence: Codeine is an opioid that acts on the central nervous system and the brain to block pain signals to the rest of the body.
note: NHS common questions about codeine and About co-codamol: affects pain receptors in the central nervous system and brain to block pain signals.

sentence: It also slows digestion, which is why it can cause constipation.
note: NHS: codeine slows down digestion, so can cause constipation.

sentence: Co-codamol adds paracetamol, another painkiller, to the codeine.
note: NHS: combination of paracetamol and codeine.

sentence: The NHS says co-codamol can take up to an hour to start working.
note: NHS About co-codamol: takes up to 1 hour to work.

sentence: Constipation, feeling sick or being sick, and feeling sleepy or tired.
note: NHS side effects pages: common effects.

sentence: Sweating.
note: NHS side effects of codeine: sweating among common effects.

sentence: Sleepiness is reported to ease within a few days as the body gets used to codeine, but constipation tends to continue.
note: NHS common questions/overview: apart from constipation, side effects tend to disappear with time; sleepiness should go away within days.

sentence: An allergic reaction, slow or shallow breathing, an unusual heartbeat or low blood pressure are listed by the NHS as uncommon serious effects; breathing difficulty or a seizure needs a 999 call.
note: NHS side effects pages: serious allergic reactions rare; call 999 for breathing difficulty or a fit. Slow breathing/heartbeat/low BP list from search summary of NHS codeine side-effects page.

sentence: Repeated use can lead to dependence, abuse and addiction, which may result in life-threatening overdose, and the risk rises with higher doses and longer use; a prescriber or pharmacist can be asked about concerns.
note: Search summary of NHS codeine page / emc leaflet: dependence, abuse, addiction; risk rises with dose and duration. Final clause is reassurance route not a sourced claim.

sentence: Stopping suddenly after regular use can cause withdrawal symptoms such as agitation, anxiety, palpitations, difficulty sleeping, shaking, sweating, body aches and restlessness, so the prescriber plans a gradual reduction.
note: NHS common questions about codeine: withdrawal on stopping suddenly; doctor reduces gradually. List from search summary.

sentence: Regular use can lead to tolerance, meaning higher amounts are needed to control pain over time.
note: NHS: tolerance with long-term use.

sentence: Codeine is not suitable for everyone: the NHS lists allergy to codeine or other medicines, lung problems, a head injury, adrenal gland problems and kidney or liver problems among reasons it may not be suitable.
note: NHS who can and cannot take codeine (via search summary).

sentence: Codeine is not given to children under 12, and the NHS says it should not be given to anyone under 18 who has had tonsils or adenoids removed for sleep apnoea.
note: NHS who can and cannot take codeine.

sentence: The NHS says codeine can be taken in pregnancy, but long-term use is not recommended, and use late in pregnancy can leave a newborn dependent so the baby may need extra observation in hospital.
note: NHS pregnancy pages for codeine and co-codamol.

sentence: The NHS says codeine and co-codamol are not taken while breastfeeding, because small amounts pass into breast milk and can cause breathing problems and drowsiness in the baby.
note: NHS pregnancy/breastfeeding pages.

sentence: Alcohol can increase the risk of side effects and make a person very sleepy.
note: NHS: best to avoid alcohol; emc leaflet: alcohol can make you very sleepy.

sentence: Recreational drugs such as cannabis, cocaine or heroin raise the risk of serious side effects with codeine.
note: NHS common questions about codeine (via search summary).

sentence: The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using tools or machinery when feeling sleepy.
note: NHS: do not drive, cycle or use machinery if sleepy; co-codamol page: do not drive if sleepy, dizzy or vision affected.

sentence: Co-codamol contains paracetamol, so other paracetamol-containing medicines, such as some cold and flu remedies, add to the total and the label of every product is checked.
note: NHS how-to / emc leaflet: do not take anything else containing paracetamol; check cold and flu remedies.

sentence: The NHS says the prescriber discusses how to lower the risk of addiction and how to reduce treatment gradually before stopping, and codeine is prescribed for the shortest time needed.
note: NHS About co-codamol: doctor will explain how to reduce addiction risk; prescribed strengths for shortest possible period (emc/search summary).
